source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: Templates are the memory side of the pattern-recognition theory. A template is a core of about a dozen pieces plus slots filled in 1-2 s. The paper restates that recognition cuts the need for look-ahead and explains good fast and simultaneous chess.
numbers: Template core about 12 pieces; chunk store 50,000 or more; skilled search tree usually under 100 positions (chunking-theory claims restated, not tested here).
quote: Recognizing familiar chunks reduces the need for 'look-ahead' search
limits: Search claims are restated theory, not data. The experiments test memory only.
agent_relevance: Supports a cheap recognition step before search: a stored pattern with slots can replace some look-ahead. Not evidence by itself that it helps an LLM.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: Exp 1: recall falls with more boards, but experts recall far more than a 7-chunk short-term store allows. First discriminating test against the original chunking model.
numbers: N=13 (3 Masters mean Elo 2453, 4 Experts 2180, 6 Class A 1883). 1 to 5 positions, 5 s each. No skill x boards interaction, F(8,40)=1.39 ns. Masters 5-board recall 50% after dropping one distracted GM.
limits: Small N. One GM lapse biased the 5-board cell. Tests memory, not move choice.
agent_relevance: A pure working-memory slot count does not explain expert performance; stored structure matters. An agent needs a long-term pattern store, not only a bigger scratchpad.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: Exp 2: longer gaps between boards raise recall, which fits slow transfer to long-term memory (templates), not a fixed short-term store.
numbers: One board: Masters 92.3% correct, Experts 64.5%; random board: Masters 21.1%, Experts 17.7%. Gain from 1 s to 10 s gap: Masters +71% (2 boards), +63% (4 boards); Experts +40% and +33%. At 10 s and 4 boards Masters replaced 82.9 of 100 pieces, Experts 44.9.
limits: The advantage almost vanishes on random boards, so it is knowledge, not general memory.
agent_relevance: Control idea: check that an agent's gain disappears on shuffled or structure-free problems.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: Exp 3: one Chessmaster trained for months with a retrieval structure and went from about 5 to 9 boards above a 60% criterion, replacing up to 160 pieces.
numbers: Single subject S. Boards above criterion: 5 to peak 9 (block 18), then 8 and 7. Pieces correct more than tripled. In one test block 80% (40 pieces) baseline to 94% (47 pieces).
limits: N=1, a member of the research team (demand risk). Gain stayed inside the usual span of boards.
agent_relevance: Deliberate retrieval structures can be trained for fast storage; analogue is an index of solved items keyed by pattern.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: Earlier interference studies disagree on what blocks chess memory. Visuospatial and executive tasks hurt, spoken 'the' did not. Charness 1976 found little interference even from visual chess tasks.
numbers: Bradley et al 1987: visuospatial or executive load cut recall by more than two thirds; tactical problem solving fell by about one third. Saariluoma 1992 replicated the visuospatial effect.
limits: Reported second-hand in the 1996 review; originals not opened.
agent_relevance: Memory-based recognition is not verbal rehearsal; evidence is mixed, so do not assume one bottleneck.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: Cooke et al 1993 multi-board work, as cited: Masters fall from about 90% with 1 board to about 50% with 5 and 40% with 9. Authors argue this exceeds what guessing or short-term memory allows.
numbers: Guessing baseline named in the paper: 43.7% of pieces placeable by chance in their set-up.
limits: Second-hand; the guess-rate argument is the authors' own.
agent_relevance: Recall scores need a guessing baseline; same for LLM tasks with small answer spaces.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess
finding: A 270M transformer trained by supervised learning on 10M human games with Stockfish action-values, with NO test-time search, plays at grandmaster level. It acts like a huge pattern store that replaces search.
numbers: Lichess blitz Elo 2895 vs humans; 2299 vs bots; tournament Elo 2299; puzzle accuracy 95.4% (10K puzzles). 9M model: 88.9% puzzles; 136M: 94.5%. AlphaZero policy net only 56.1%, value net only 82.0%, with 400 MCTS sims 95.6%. Only 1.33% of puzzles overlap training.
quote: Our searchless chess policy solves challenging chess puzzles
limits: Strength depends on engine-labelled data (Stockfish 16 oracle). Elo vs bots lower than vs humans (pool effects). Cannot plan ahead; puzzles solved by greedy value estimates. Not an LLM reading text.
agent_relevance: Strongest recent evidence that recognition alone can stand in for search when the store is huge and well labelled. Shortening works only if the stored knowledge is good.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess
finding: Scale test: more data and a bigger model both raise puzzle accuracy; with small data (10K games) models of 7M+ parameters overfit.
numbers: Grid over 10K, 100K, 1M games and model size; puzzle accuracy rises with both. Sizes 9M, 136M, 270M monotone in all metrics.
limits: Ablations at 9M scale; other scales inferred.
agent_relevance: Pattern-store quality scales with data volume: a small hand-made exemplar bank will be thin.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess
finding: Text-LLM comparison: GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct (PGN input) is far behind the searchless net.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct puzzle accuracy 66.5%, Lichess Elo 1755 (vs bots). 270M net: 95.4% and 2299.
limits: Different training regime; authors say comparisons are for orientation only.
agent_relevance: Base LLM recognition is far weaker than trained recognition; do not assume expert-level patterns in the base model.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess
finding: Leela Chess Zero: its policy net alone is already strong, and search still adds a margin. Recognition shortens search but does not remove it.
numbers: Leela policy only: tournament Elo 2292, puzzles 88.6%; value only 2418, 95.9%; 400 MCTS sims 2858, 99.6%. Stockfish 16 at 50 ms: 2711, 99.8%; at 1.5 s: 100%.
limits: Different inputs and training; not a controlled test of templates.
agent_relevance: A fast recognition pass then a check on hard cases fits the S0 gate idea.

source: Jenner et al. (2024) Evidence of learned look-ahead in a chess-playing neural network
finding: A pattern-trained network (Leela transformer policy) seems to compute future moves internally. Recognition and search are not cleanly separate inside a network.
numbers: Patching the 3rd-move target square cuts log-odds of the correct move by 1.88 +/- 0.04 (2 SE) in layer 10. Zeroing one attention entry cuts log-odds by 1.5+ in over 10% of puzzles. Blocking info out of the 3rd-move square in piece-movement heads: 1.5+ drop in 60% of puzzles. Probe predicts 3rd move at 92%.
limits: Only puzzles Leela solves with a unique line; 83% of filtered puzzles have equal 1st and 2nd target square vs 47% unfiltered (selection bias). Existence proof. Leela is not a language model.
agent_relevance: Weakens a clean 'recognition replaces search' story. A prompt that skips explicit search may still hide look-ahead.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent world models and latent variable estimation in chess-playing language models
finding: A GPT trained only on chess move text builds a linear board-state code and estimates player skill as a latent variable used to predict the next move.
numbers: Board-state intervention lifts legal-move rate from 41% (original model on modified board) to 92%; 5,000 cases, 5 samples each, temperature 1.0. Elo probe labelled 99.4% of 4,000 random-init games as low skill. Skill-vector edits kept over 98% legal moves.
limits: Small models (25M and 50M parameters). A single-layer fix at layer 4 gives 85.5% in the 8-layer model.
agent_relevance: The model infers whose play it imitates from context; state the target level explicitly in prompts.

source: Toshniwal et al. (2022) Chess as a testbed for language model state tracking
finding: Transformers trained on move strings can track piece locations and predict legal moves given enough data and a piece-location aid (RAP).
numbers: UCI+RAP legal start-square accuracy perfect with the large training set, 91.3% with the small; non-moved piece location 99.6%; legal-move accuracy over 97% for UCI and UCI+RAP.
limits: Only the results section was read; small models; legality is not move quality.
agent_relevance: Pattern use needs reliable state tracking first; add a code-checked legality step before search.

source: McIlroy-Young et al. (2020) Aligning superhuman AI with human behavior: chess as a model system (Maia)
finding: Stronger engines do not predict human moves better. Networks trained on human games at one rating match moves of players near that rating, a rating-specific pattern store.
numbers: Maia best move-match accuracy over 52%; worst cell (trained 1900, tested 1100) 46%, as good as the best Stockfish or Leela. Prediction curves peak near training rating. Inter-Maia agreement 65% to 79%.
limits: Move prediction, not strength; Lichess blitz pool.
agent_relevance: A scaffold built from human-like patterns differs from one built from best-engine moves.

source: Lehnert et al. (2024) Beyond A*: better planning with transformers via search dynamics bootstrapping (Searchformer)
finding: A transformer trained on search traces and then bootstrapped solves Sokoban optimally with fewer search steps than the teacher: a learned heuristic that shortens search.
numbers: Solves unseen Sokoban 93.7%; up to 26.8% fewer search steps than the A* used for training; beats direct-answer baselines with 5-10x smaller model and 10x smaller data.
limits: Synthetic grid tasks with checkable optimum; not chess or free text. Only abstract and introduction read.
agent_relevance: Direct analogue of 'templates shorten search': learned guidance cut steps by about a quarter. Candidate test in our loop.

source: Gobet (1997) A pattern-recognition theory of search in expert problem solving
finding: Template theory of search: retrieved templates supply plausible moves and evaluation so search is selective and short. Only existence and DOI confirmed via Crossref metadata.
numbers: Not read.
limits: [M] from memory, source not opened this session; verify before use. Full text not accessed (paywalled; search tools blocked or out of quota).
agent_relevance: Key paper for this subfield; needs a proper read before the schema relies on it.

source: de Groot (1946/1965) Thought and choice in chess
finding: Masters and weaker players looked at a similar amount of search; masters found the best move more often; early fixation on the first plausible line was common.
numbers: Not verified.
